name: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine (MMR)

immune_when.reason: You told us a healthcare professional or blood test confirmed you're immune to measles, mumps and rubella.
immune_when.section: Measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination: evidence of immunity

indications.reason: Healthcare workers born in 1957 or later without evidence of immunity should have 2 doses of MMR at least 4 weeks apart.
indications.section: Measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination: Special situations (healthcare personnel)

indications.reason: Students after high school, international travellers, and close contacts of people with weakened immune systems should have 2 doses of MMR if they don't have evidence of immunity.
indications.section: Measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination: Special situations

indications.reason: Adults born in 1957 or later without evidence of immunity to measles, mumps or rubella need at least 1 dose of MMR.
indications.section: Measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination: Routine vaccination

indications.reason: Being born before 1957 usually counts as evidence of immunity, but for healthcare workers a 2-dose MMR series should be considered.
indications.section: Measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination: Special situations (healthcare personnel)

not_indicated_reason: Being born before 1957 counts as evidence of immunity to measles, mumps and rubella for most adults.

contraindications.text: A severe allergic reaction (such as anaphylaxis) after a previous dose, or to a vaccine ingredient.

Severe immunodeficiency, for example from blood or solid tumours, chemotherapy, long-term immunosuppressive treatment, a congenital immunodeficiency, or severely weakened immunity from HIV. MMR is a live vaccine.
A family history of immune system problems, unless your own immune system has been confirmed as normal by a clinician or test.
Pregnancy. MMR should not be given during pregnancy. If you're not immune to rubella, one dose is recommended after the pregnancy.
contraindications.section: Measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination: Special situations (pregnancy)

precautions.text: Receiving an antibody-containing blood product in the last 11 months.
A history of low platelet count (thrombocytopenia or thrombocytopenic purpura).
A moderate or severe illness right now, with or without fever.

content.disease: Measles causes fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, commonly followed by a rash. Mumps causes fever, headache, muscle aches, tiredness, loss of appetite and swollen, tender salivary glands. Rubella causes fever, sore throat, rash, headache and eye irritation.
content.why: Adults without evidence of immunity can catch and spread these infections. Rubella during pregnancy can harm the baby, so immunity before pregnancy matters.
content.who: Adults born in 1957 or later without evidence of immunity. Two doses for healthcare workers, students after high school, international travellers and close contacts of people with weakened immune systems.
content.doses_text: One or two doses, at least 4 weeks apart, depending on your situation.
content.catch_up: Written records of MMR doses, a blood test showing immunity, or (for most adults) being born before 1957 count as evidence of immunity.
common_reactions: Sore arm or redness where the shot was given
serious_reactions: A temporary low platelet count, which can cause unusual bleeding or bruising
A severe allergic reaction is very rare.
